titleStmt.title: Telegram From the Department of State to the Embassy in Uruguay

div.head: 446. Telegram From the Department of State to the Embassy in Uruguay
div.p: 313724. Subject: Meeting with Colorado Party Leader Dr. Julio Sanguinetti.

2. Summary: On October 11 HA Assistant Secretary Elliott Abrams met with Colorado Party Leader Dr. Julio Sanguinetti. Sanguinetti reviewed recent political developments in Uruguay and commented on the now suspended political negotiations with the military. He expressed concern for the problems created by the personal ambitions of President Alvarez. Sanguinetti commented that the practice of maltreatment and torture of political detainees continues, although he believes that the number of incidents has declined. He stated that a majority of the leaders of both political parties believe that the proscription of a few prominent politicians such as Wilson Ferreira should not be permitted to block an accord with the military. Sanguinetti opined that US policy toward Uruguay has been good and the US should not act in a manner that would affect its ability to influence the GOU. Sanguinetti said that many political prisoners have been imprisoned for periods disproportionate to the seriousness of their crimes, and they should be released, whereas others would be in jail for their serious crimes under any government. He also said that he did not consider the human rights organization Servicio Paz Y Justicia to be subversive, but said he keeps his distance from them because some of their leaders had previously expressed sympathy for the Tupamaros. End summary.

3. Colorado Party Secretary General, Dr. Julio Sanguinetti, met with HA Assistant Secretary Elliott Abrams and HA officers on October 11. After a brief statement by Abrams expressing US support for the democratization process in Uruguay, Sanguinetti said that after ten years of problems in the area of human rights
under this military government there have been some recent improvements. Many problems continue, however, particularly in the areas of freedom of the press, freedom of association and mistreatment of detained individuals. Sanguinetti added that human rights is part of the general problem in Uruguay. When the democratization process is brought to a successful conclusion, the question of human rights will automatically be resolved.

4. Sanguinetti reviewed developments in Uruguay since the defeat of the 1980 draft constitution. He said that the current talks between the military and the political parties regarding amendments to the constitution, broke down on July 5 because the military insisted on retaining a number of prerogatives, such as the right to cordon off an area to search for suspects and the right to invade homes at night. There were a total of twenty-four proposed amendments that were unacceptable.

5. Sanguinetti said that the parties expected that, as part of this dialogue with the military, the number of people proscribed would decrease; instead the number of proscriptions has increased. This made it impossible for the political parties to continue with the dialogue or to resume it once it was stopped. The military had tried to get the political parties to resume talks, and some senior military officials visited Sanguinetti recently at his home just before his departure for the U.S. in an effort to convince him to resume the discussions, but Sanguinetti explained to the generals that the atmosphere generated by the proscription of Eladio Fernandez and by the closing of the weekly publications made this impossible. Sanguinetti said that the military did not seem to understand that proscriptions were an important issue and that these actions made it impossible for the political parties to justify to their rank and file a return to the political dialogue. Sanguinetti continued that before a dialogue can resume, the military must take actions such as ending Constitutional Act No. 7, which allows the government to fire any public employee for political reasons, and ending the practice of closing newspapers. He continued that the political parties are willing to run the risk of antagonizing the military in order to obtain some concessions before returning to the bargaining table.

6. Sanguinetti said that the worst thing the military can do would be to interrupt the political process. This would do to the Uruguayan military what the Malvinas defeat did for the Argentine military (inferring that they would be totally discredited in public opinion).

7. Sanguinetti then reviewed the differences between President Alvarez and the rest of the military. He said that Alvarez is personally responsible for the recent
banning and the closing of the journals, and he takes a far harder position than do the rest of the senior officers in the military. According to Sanguinetti, 90 percent of the problem in reaching agreement with the military is a result of the personal ambition of President Alvarez, and Alvarez himself encourages the other 10 percent of the problem which is caused by military fear of change. Since some officers have been tried in Argentina, the military has a natural fear, encouraged by Alvarez, that the Uruguayan political parties would try to do the same thing once democracy is restored in Uruguay. The political party leaders have talked very frankly with the military saying that they do not intend to take any revenge for previous actions, but Alvarez has told them that the parties may not be able to control their rank and file.

8. Asked to go into some more detail on the prevalence of torture, Sanguinetti said that torture has not been eliminated but the number of incidents has decreased. He said that dictatorships generally create situations in which there is little respect among the police for the people. Moreover, there are certain police groups which use torture in their fight against terrorists. Since terrorism has declined, the use of torture has declined as well. Nevertheless, two months ago a group of youthful communist activists started to organize themselves and were arrested and placed before a military court. This was wrong because they were neither terrorists nor members of the military and therefore should have been tried by civil authorities. Sanguinetti stated that they were definitely maltreated while in the custody of the military, thereby demonstrating that torture still does occur.

9. On the subject of Wilson Ferreira, Sanguinetti said the Ferreira question is one of the most serious problems to be resolved between the politicians and the military. The military are insistent that they will not accept his return to political life. Sanguinetti believes that the Colorado Party as well as a majority of the Blanco Party, including the leadership of the party, are in agreement that the question of the political status of one or two people like Wilson Ferreira cannot be allowed to stand in the way of reaching an agreement with the military on a return to democratic government. Sanguinetti added that he recently had met with Ferreira in Bolivia and, not surprisingly, Ferreira did not agree. Ferreira believes that the Colorado Party would prefer to have him outside the country because it would then be easier for the Colorados to win their election. Sanguinetti differed, saying that he beat Ferreira in 1971 and it would be easier to beat him again then to run against Ferreira’s stand-in, who could exploit the political issue of Ferreira’s proscription. Asked about the Colorado Party leader, Jorge Batlle, Sanguinetti said that like Ferreira, Batlle remains banned, but he does live in Montevideo and despite legal proscriptions against him does participate normally in internal
Colorado Party activities. He cannot, however, be a candidate in the 1984 elections. Asked whether he thought the proscription against Batlle might be removed, Sanguinetti replied that if the proscription against Juan Ferreira remained in effect, for purposes of balance the proscription against Batlle would probably remain in effect. Sanguinetti continued that he has told Wilson Ferreira’s son, Juan, that it might be best for ten people to remain proscribed than for the democratization process to be torpedoed as a result.

10. Asked for his opinion of U.S. policy and U.S. public statements on the movement toward democratic government in Uruguay, Sanguinetti responded that he thought the U.S. position has been a good one. The U.S., he said, should act in a way that will not affect its ability to influence the GOU. Sanguinetti then recalled that under President Carter the U.S. used to criticize the GOU publicly. This angered the military but made the people happy. With the election of President Reagan the military were happy, and in fact the Navy Commander said that the Carter nightmare was over. The Uruguayan military were then surprised at the position of the Reagan Administration. In particular he considered a U.S. statement issued after the August 2, 1983 suspension of public political activity to be excellent. Although the military prohibited the daily newspapers from publishing it, the influential weekly political journals, which operate in a legally nebulous area, published the statement, and the government did not retaliate. Sanguinetti added that at times the political parties would like the U.S. to exert more pressure, but they realize that the U.S. cannot do so without losing its influence with the GOU.

11. Asked about the status of political prisoners in Uruguay, Sanguinetti said that he divides them into three categories. The first consists of typical political prisoners, such as General Seregni, who was a leftist candidate for President in 1971. He was later arrested and accused of participating in a public disturbance in 1973 and of being a traitor because, as a military officer, he joined the Communist Party. Sanguinetti said that Seregni’s crime warranted a maximum of 6 months in prison, maybe even a year if it were a very serious disturbance, but certainly not 8 years in prison. A democratic government would let people like Seregni out immediately, and it would be far better for the military to begin this process while they are still in office.

12. The second category consists of those people who would be imprisoned under any government because of their having participated in violent acts such as terrorism. These cases, however, should be reviewed and the number reduced to the bare minimum. The third group consists of prisoners who may have belonged to
subversive organizations but who either did not receive a fair trial or who have already served their sentences. A democratic government would have all these cases reviewed and liberate most of these people.

13. Asked to comment on the cases of Massera and Hiber Conteras, Sanguinetti said that he is very familiar with Massera and in fact served in the Congress with him. Massera is a communist mathematician who attended Berkeley and is now 65 years old. Sanguinetti opined that he clearly falls in the first category. He has never been accused of any crime other than of being a member of the Communist Party which was a legal party when he was a member.

14. Sanguinetti said that he was not very familiar with the Conteras case. He knows that Conteras was a writer and a journalist, but although he read some of his material he never met him. He believes that Conteras would fall in the third category and a judge should review his case.

15. On the subject of human rights groups, Sanguinetti said that the recently formed Human Rights Commission is composed of important and prestigious democratic personalities such as Dr. Reta, a former university professor and specialist in penal law, who is no longer allowed to teach at the university. This newly formed group has not yet done anything, but it will be important simply because of the prominence of its members.

16. Regarding Servicio Paz y Justicio, Sanguinetti said it is composed of people who have taken a more confrontational position. The Colorado Party shares their general views but has reservations about the group because some of them, such as Father Perez Aguirre, were sympathetic to the Tupamaros during the terrorist period. Although they were not then nor are now a subversive group, Sanguinetti said he has kept his distance from them because of their political leanings.

note.p: Source: Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D830643–0855. Confidential. Sent for information to Buenos Aires. Drafted by Snyder; cleared in HA/HR and HA; approved by Abrams.

In telegram 4244 from Montevideo, August 3, the Embassy reported: “The GOU announced August 2 a decision to limit public political activity, control political reporting and commentary, and extend the applicability of rules concerning proscription. Announcement also reiterated government’s commitment to hold elections in 1984 for a government to take office March 1985.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D830442–0755)

In telegram 4283 from Montevideo, November 1, 1982, the Embassy sent a lengthy review of Álvarez’s “mixed record” after his first year as President: “While his inaugural promises have been partially fulfilled, his administration in many respects is hardly distinguishable from its lackluster predecessor. In foreign policy, the GOU played a useful moderating role during the South Atlantic crisis; bilateral relations took a downward turn during the conflict but have improved in recent months. On the economic front, Uruguay under Alvarez has had great difficulty developing coherent policies to deal with the country’s severe recession. With internal party elections scheduled for the end of November, Alvarez continues to hold to his commitment to restore elected government to Uruguay in 1985.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D82565–0246)

In telegram 219613 to multiple posts, August 4, the Department sent the text of press guidance calling the Uruguayan suspension of political activities “potential obstacles to democracy in Uruguay” and “cause for particular concern,” while noting the Uruguayan Government’s “renewed commitment” to 1984 elections and its “declaration that the armed forces are open to a dialogue with Uruguay’s political parties.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D830446–0230)
